scope: Primary literature and official repositories only; no DZMM interaction, attack execution, or generation API calls

papers.title: Just Ask: Curious Code Agents Reveal System Prompts in Frontier LLMs
papers.access: Standard chat API with text input/output and repeated queries; no target weights, logits or hidden states. Code agent orchestrates the attack. Separate Claude Code case involves its subagent interface.
papers.training: No labeled training set or model fine-tuning; updates strategy statistics online.
papers.benchmark: 41 OpenRouter model endpoints, 20 attempts/model. Reported 100% success means mean self/cross-strategy embedding consistency >=0.7. External checks: Grok official disclosure cosine similarity 0.89; Claude Code Explore prompt vs decompilation 0.94. Known-prompt controlled study is separate.
papers.caveat: Consistency is not ground-truth exact match. README currently says 45 models; conference abstract and read v1 say 41. This discrepancy is preserved.

papers.title: RepeatLeakage: Leak Prompts from Repeating as Large Language Model Is a Good Repeater
papers.access: Attack is text-only. Mechanistic validation used white-box activation interventions; that instrumentation is not required for the proposed query method.
papers.training: No attacker model training required for template use.
papers.benchmark: 90 filtered English system prompts; Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Phi-3-Small-8K-Instruct, Qwen2-7B-Instruct with default generation. System-prompt BERTScore 99–100% band: 68.9%, 77.8%, 72.2% respectively (Table 3).
papers.caveat: Similarity bands are not exact-string recovery; public leaked-prompt corpus provenance and English/open-model setup limit inference to a Chinese commercial service.

papers.title: PLeak: Prompt Leaking Attacks against Large Language Model Applications
papers.access: Target is black box. Offline optimization requires a differentiable shadow LLM and known shadow system prompts; gradients are not from the target.
papers.mechanism: Incrementally optimize queries toward longer prompt prefixes; transfer several queries and aggregate responses.
papers.benchmark: 50 Poe apps; four queries optimized with LLaMA-2 and Roles prompts. Reported EM: one query 42%, multiple queries 68%; Table 5.
papers.caveat: Requires offline optimization or previously optimized queries. Transfer to different defenses, language and dynamic prompt assembly is uncertain; full response may include extra text even when EM succeeds.

papers.title: PRSA: Prompt Stealing Attacks against Real-World Prompt Services
papers.access: Limited input-output examples plus an auxiliary LLM; no target logits or weights. Default generating LLM matches target family.
papers.training: Auxiliary corpus approximately 50 prompts per each of 18 categories; prompt-generation optimization is not target weight access.
papers.benchmark: 360 purchased PromptBase prompts (180 GPT-3.5, 180 GPT-4) and 100 selected GPT Store apps. GPT-4 marketplace ASR 46.1% vs prior 17.8%; Store 52% vs 39%. ASR tests output semantic >=0.75, syntactic >=0.75, structural >=0.9 consistency.
papers.caveat: Functional reconstruction; ASR is not original prompt exact match. Unknown DZMM backend weakens matching-model assumption.

papers.title: Extracting Prompts by Inverting LLM Outputs
papers.access: Only normal text outputs; no target logits, gradients, logit bias or adversarial queries.
papers.training: Requires trained sparse-encoder inversion model. System-prompt experiment uses 25K synthetic GPT prompts for training, GPT-3.5 outputs, four queries yielding 64 short outputs.
papers.benchmark: Read v1, Table 4: held-out Synthetic GPTs without extra finetuning cosine 98.1, BLEU 36.8; transfer to Awesome-ChatGPT-Prompts without finetuning cosine 83.9, BLEU 2.1. These quantify similarity, not exact system-prompt recovery.
papers.caveat: v1 says its simulated system prompt occupies first assistant turn; role hierarchy setup must be checked before transfer. Adaptive prompts and in-context examples can remain unrecoverable. Conference metadata and v1 numerical version are distinguished.

papers.title: On the Effectiveness of Prompt Stealing Attacks on In-The-Wild Prompts
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2025, 392–410
papers.access: Text outputs and auxiliary generation/evaluation LLM; no target logits needed by T-GPS. Default experiments use same target/attacker GPT-3.5-turbo-0125.
papers.mechanism: Iterative text-gradient feedback on output discrepancies with beam search over candidate reconstructed prompts.
papers.benchmark: 421 prompt-output pairs sampled after filtering 15,140 wild prompts to 1,855. Table 2/3 GPT-3.5 T-GPS METEOR prompt 0.253, output 0.440; grouped PRSA 0.207, 0.323. Three repetitions per method.
papers.caveat: Placeholders excluded, also prompts longer than their outputs. Similar outputs can originate from many distinct prompts. Scores are neither exact recovery nor universal attack success.

recommended_verification: Separate verbatim recovery, semantic reconstruction and behavioral imitation.
Independent original prompt or official diagnostic is strongest ground truth.
Cross-session agreement is supporting evidence, not proof; control for user-seeded contamination and generic boilerplate.
Do not use self-reported vendor identity as model attribution.
